claim: The runner's memory guard now watches the host, not one process. tools/runner reads system-wide available memory before each sample and, below a danger floor derived from hw.memsize (total // 8, override --host-mem-floor-mb, disable --no-host-guard), SIGKILLs the LARGEST member of the process group — a fleet citizen relieving host pressure before the host panics, naming the process, its RSS, and the free-memory figure. The per-process --rss-cap-mb is retained as a secondary bound, generously redefaulted to 12288 MB (was 4096) so a legitimate 4.1 GB check is no longer blocked but a single runaway allocation still is. The progress watchdog is unchanged. The 2026-07-29 watchdog-timeout kernel panic (system free ~46 MB of 48 GB, docs/infra/host/incident-2026-07-29.md) is the cited precedent in the code.

design.defect: tools/runner's --rss-cap-mb was per-process and absolute: it bounded ONE worker and said nothing about five at once. The host has 48 GB and has already taken a watchdog-timeout kernel panic under OOM (2026-07-29). On 2026-08-04 the operator raised two rows to 8192 MB because 4096 blocked complete implementations by 0.1% and 2% — correct for one row, and five such rows would commit 40 GB.
design.host_guard: Before each poll, _host_avail_bytes() reads system-wide available memory (macOS vm_stat: free+inactive+purgeable+speculative, page size parsed from the header line; Linux /proc/meminfo MemAvailable). When it falls below the danger floor, the guard finds the largest member of the process group by current RSS (poll_rss, collected in the existing RSS loop), SIGKILLs that single pid (surgical — not the whole group), and logs '[runner] KILL: host memory pressure — avail N MB < floor M MB' plus '[runner]   killed largest member: pid P RSS R MB'. If the largest member is the direct child (proc.pid), the run ends via the existing exit-124 path; otherwise the loop continues and, if pressure persists, the next poll kills the next-largest. The floor is derived from hw.memsize (total // 8 ≈ 6 GB on 48 GB) unless --host-mem-floor-mb overrides; --no-host-guard disables. The reading is injectable via WEIZIGO_HOST_MEM_AVAIL_MB so the danger floor is NEVER tested by actually exhausting host memory (the brief's bar).
design.secondary_bound: --rss-cap-mb default raised 4096 → 12288. The per-process cap now stops a runaway allocation (the 2026-07-29 zig blowup was 12.5 GB resident / 21.8 GB peak), not a legitimate 4.1 GB check. The division of labor: the per-process cap catches a single runaway; the host guard catches fleet composition (five 8 GB rows = 40 GB).
design.progress_watchdog_unchanged: The progress watchdog (--progress-timeout) and the wall/CPU fallback ceilings are untouched. The host guard is checked in its own block before the kill-decision chain and only sets kill_reason when the direct child is the largest; surgical grandchild kills do not interfere with stuck-detection.
